tasks.title: Battery failsafe posture, review and approve the BMS capacity based values (yes or no)
tasks.doneWhen: Two answers on the record in this issue: (1) yes or no on the low and critical values below, (2) yes or no on the arming block, judged on its own. A no comes with the number you would use instead and why.
tasks.body:
**Task board row T-01** (see `tasks.md`)

| | |
|---|---|
| Price | $75 |
| Funding line | QGB-FLEX (open task pool) |
| Owner | Julius |
| Deadline | 2026-09-30 |
| Done when | Two answers on the record in this issue: (1) yes or no on the low and critical values below, (2) yes or no on the arming block, judged on its own. A no comes with the number you would use instead and why. |

**What is being asked**

Review the proposed battery failsafe posture below and approve or reject it. The design work is done, the numbers are chosen, and the documentation carries them as proposed changes (Pilot's Handbook §4.2.1, Initial Configuration Guide §7.3 and §7.4). No parameter file is cut until this issue closes with a yes. You own the battery PCB and the pack integration, so this is your call to check.

**The proposal**

Bat2 (the Tattu 4.0 pack's own BMS, GBMS063E12, DroneCAN node 125) becomes the primary failsafe source on consumed capacity. Bat1 (ESC monitor, voltage) stays as the backstop.

| Parameter | Today (911 card) | Proposed | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `BATT2_LOW_MAH` | 6000 | 7500 | Low stage at 25 percent remaining |
| `BATT2_FS_LOW_ACT` | 0 | 0 during the OA campaign, 2 (RTL) after RTL plus obstacle avoidance is validated in Test 5 | Warn now, return home later |
| `BATT2_CRT_MAH` | 0 | 4500 | Critical stage at 15 percent remaining |
| `BATT2_FS_CRT_ACT` | 1 | 1 | Land in place, unchanged |
| `BATT2_LOW_VOLT` / `BATT2_CRT_VOLT` | 46.2 / 44.8 | unchanged | 3.3 and 3.2 V per cell, last line on Bat2 |
| Bat1 (`BATT_*`) | 46.2 warn / 44.8 land, sag compensated | unchanged | Independent backstop if the BMS stops reporting |

**Second question, judged separately: an arming block**

`BATT2_ARM_MAH` 0 to 9000 would refuse arming with less than 30 percent remaining. Because the BMS count persists across boots, a pack installed half used would be caught. The lead has not adopted this into the Handbook or the guide yet. Say yes or no to it on its own. A yes adds it to the same card revision.

**Why capacity on the BMS and not voltage on the ESC**

1. The BMS coulomb count is validated. On September 3 the charger restored 23,889 mAh into a pack whose BMS had counted 25,476 mAh consumed, 93.8 percent, inside normal charge efficiency. The count is accurate.
2. The BMS sees the whole aircraft. Bat1 sums the four ESCs and never sees the avionics, the Pi, the radios, or the sensors. On the same flight Bat2 reads about 22 percent more consumed than Bat1 (log 45: 26,106 vs 21,291 mAh, log 47: 27,365 vs 22,377 mAh). That gap is the avionics load, not an error, and it is exactly the energy a voltage only failsafe on the ESC monitor does not account for.
3. The count persists across power cycles. The BMS reports consumed since last charge over DroneCAN and the flight controller does not reset it at boot (logs 48 to 49, same pack: ended 7,652, restarted 7,840 mAh). A pack installed half used arms with the correct remaining figure. The ESC counter starts from zero every boot.
4. The pack does not sag enough for voltage to be an early trigger. At the capacity trip in log 47 (24,005 mAh consumed, 22.3 minutes airborne) the pack read 48.75 V raw, 3.48 V per cell. A voltage threshold high enough to fire before the capacity stage would fire under heavy mass and make the capacity logic pointless.
5. Flight 10 (July 30) proved the capacity failsafe works as configured: the Bat2 stage commanded RTL at 20.7 minutes and the aircraft came home. The low stage was moved to warn only afterwards because that RTL was the first autonomous mode ever engaged on the aircraft and the path planner came with it. That reason expires when Test 5 (RTL plus obstacle avoidance) passes.

**How the reserve was sized**

Hover draw on the BMS is 50 to 80 A, so one minute costs roughly 1,100 mAh. A return from the 60 m fence boundary at mission speed, the landing, and a 6 percent counter error band come to about 5,000 mAh. 7,500 mAh (25 percent) covers that with margin for pack ageing and a heavier payload. 4,500 mAh (15 percent) is the point where the aircraft lands itself with no pilot discretion. Hover flights currently end at the 6,000 mAh warning around 22 minutes, so the low stage moves about two minutes earlier.

**Known Bat2 quirks, judged not to block this**

The BMS reports discharge current with a negative sign, `CurrTot` advances in coarse steps, and `VoltR` and `Res` stay at zero (guide open item 8). None of these affect the consumed count the failsafe reads. If you disagree, say so here.

**Your answer**

Yes on question 1: the low and critical numbers go into the next parameter card (912) as a controlled revision alongside the AUTO phase changes, and the Handbook and guide text loses its "proposed" marker.
No on question 1: give the values you would set and the reason, and the documentation is updated to match.
Question 2 (arming block) is adopted or dropped on its own answer.

Source: `docs/Operations/Initial-Configuration-Guide.md` §7.3, §7.4, §17.8, open item 8. `2026 OA Testing/oa-next-steps-2026-09-10.md` §5 decision 6. Decision taken by the Project Lead 2026-09-10.

**Acceptance and payment**
Payment lands on acceptance by the Project Lead. Payouts batch monthly through the CSV airdrop flow. Board rules in `tasks.md`.

**The flights, flown by the Project Lead**

The March test matrix holds: no payload, 5 kg, 7 kg, each flown as a hover and as a circle, six flights. Two changes from the March text. The circle is a flown AUTO mission, not a manual orbit, so it is repeatable across masses and it doubles as post Test 5 autonomous time. And the existing record flights (logs 47 and 79, no payload hover, 25.2 and 20.7 minutes) already give the no payload hover point, so the new work is the four payload flights and the two circles, with one fresh no payload hover only if the pack or the airframe has changed since log 47.

Each flight runs to the low battery stage (25 percent remaining under the posture in #248, 20 percent until that closes), lands, and records the mass on the airframe, the pack serial, the ambient temperature, and the wind. Site is the Houston backyard used for the OA campaign. Payload mounting is the lead's problem to solve before the first payload flight.

The flying is compensated from the 10,000 $ARROW Flight Test Campaign pool per validated log, under the V1 campaign mechanics being defined in #263. It is not paid from this bounty and it is not covered by the retainer's flight operations scope, because these are campaign flights with a defined deliverable. The lead accepts $ARROW for them.

**The study, by KBM**

From the six logs plus the two record flights, using the multi log viewer or Mission Planner, whichever holds up:

1. Endurance versus takeoff mass, hover and circle, as a table and one chart.
2. Energy per minute by flight phase (takeoff, hover or cruise, descent) from the BMS instance (Bat2), which sees the whole aircraft. Note the ESC instance (Bat1) beside it so the avionics share is visible.
3. Hover current versus mass, and the hover throttle the flight controller learned at each mass.
4. One paragraph on what the 25 percent reserve buys at each mass, in minutes.
5. The method: which log fields, which instance, how phases were cut, so the next person can repeat it on the next airframe.

**The job**

The Pilot's Handbook was written before the aircraft had flown. Since July it has flown more than forty times across two operators, an obstacle avoidance campaign, an endurance record, one battery failsafe return, and a set of attachment tests, and none of that is in the Handbook except two sections the Project Lead wrote himself. The lead does not have the hours to do the rest. This task is for someone to go and get it out of the pilots' heads and into the book.

**How it works**

1. **Read the record first.** The first unit commissioning record, the OA campaign folder (`2026 OA Testing/`), the flight tracking platform records, and the two sections already updated (§2.5.5 post shipment recalibration, §4.2.1 battery failsafe). You should arrive at every interview knowing what the logs say happened.
2. **Interview every pilot who has flown a Quiver.** The Project Lead (Houston, most of the flights), Thomas (West Texas), and the second operator once they have missions. Forty five minutes each, recorded with consent, on a question list you write from step 1 and post in this issue before the first interview. The questions that matter most: what did you do that the Handbook does not say, what did the Handbook say that you did differently and why, what surprised you, and what would you tell the next pilot on day one.
3. **Write the changes.** Every procedure that changed, every warning that was earned, every number that moved. Known items waiting for you, so you are not starting blind: the RTL recovery procedure (a channel 9 edge exits RTL, channel 10 high recommands it, learned on flight 10), the path planner note (BendyRuler arrives with any autonomous mode and steers around obstacles it sees, which surprised the pilot on that same flight), the preflight rule on motor arm screws and latches, the open sky GPS soak while the interference investigation runs, the MK32 warm up and the USB COM versus Remote ID exclusivity, the pilot takeover briefing before any AUTO run from the OA campaign, and the abort criteria from the OA test plan.
4. **Reconcile with the rest.** Where the Handbook and the Initial Configuration Guide disagree, say which one is right in the PR and fix the Handbook side. The docs backlog (`docs-update-backlog.md`, section 1) lists ten known Handbook defects, most of them one line fixes. Close them in the same PR.
5. **Deliver.** One PR against `docs/Operations/Pilot-Handbook.md` with a change log at the top of the PR description: change, source (flight number, log, or interviewee), section. The lead reviews the technical content, the pilots you interviewed confirm you heard them right.

**Why the interviews and not just the logs**

The logs say what the aircraft did. Only the pilot knows what they were thinking, what they nearly did, and what they would do differently. The Handbook exists for the next pilot, and the next pilot needs the second thing.

**Acceptance and payment**
Payment lands on acceptance by the Project Lead when the PR merges. Payouts batch monthly through the CSV airdrop flow. If the second operator has not flown by the end of October, the task proceeds with the two pilots available and the third interview becomes a follow up at retro rates. Board rules in `tasks.md`.

**Task board row T-05** (see `tasks.md`)

| | |
|---|---|
| Price | $750 in three milestones: M1 $250, M2 $350, M3 $150 (below) |
| Funding line | QGB-01 Attachment Developer Guide line, open since May 2026 |
| Owner | OPEN. Reviewers: Thomas (integrator, he asked for this guide in May and built two attachments with it missing), Erick (electrical). |
| Deadline | M1 2026-10-10, M2 2026-10-24, M3 2026-10-31 |
| Done when | `docs/Develop-Attachments-Software/Attachment-Developer-Guide.md` is merged, passes the link checker and cspell, and both reviewers have signed off in this issue. |

**The job in one sentence**

Write the one document a third party reads to build a Quiver attachment: how to get a payload connected physically, connected electrically without browning out the aircraft, and talking to the flight controller and the Hub software.

**This is compilation, not research**

Nearly every fact the guide needs already exists. It is scattered across two GitHub issues, a KiCad project, a netlist, the configuration guide, the SDK guide, three org repositories, six attachment requirement documents, and three attachments built at the August meetup. The author's work is to read all of it, resolve the contradictions by going to the schematic, and write the contract down once. This issue is the complete brief. There is no other scope document.

**Sources you will work from**

- Issue #233: the pogo array, the signal set, the HV battery taps, the DroneCAN adapter board pattern.
- Issue #234: the power truth. The 12 V payload rail is about 13 W shared across all three ports, `12VSW` exists on the bottom port only, and high power attachments go to the switched HV path.
- `src/pcb/attach_pcb/QuiverAttachPCB` V1.4 KiCad and the Main PCB netlist: the per port pinout. Three facts the author must carry that the silkscreen gets wrong: the aux signal is `FMU_CH1` on the bottom port but `FMU_CH7` and `FMU_CH8` on the side ports (servo outputs 9, 15, 16), the bottom and side 1 ports sit on CAN1, the flight critical bus, and only side 2 is on CAN2. Payload Ethernet is 100BASE-TX, pairs A and B only. There is no GPS timepulse line to any bay, the aux channel is the timing path.
- Initial Configuration Guide §11.6 (PWM on the aux channels, the `SERVO_GPIO_MASK` bits to clear), the relay table (Pilot Handbook §2.8.5), the SSR power hierarchy.
- SDK Developer Guide: the software side, link it, do not duplicate it. Payload IP range `.100` to `.199`, bottom port `.100`. Note: the address table on `main` is stale until the repo sync lands (CubeNode `.50`, Pi `.49`, FC `.51`). Use the corrected values and cite the sync PR.
- Org repositories: `payload-systems` (open source payload designs), `quiver-payload-template` (the starting point for a payload app), `quiver-sdk` (the Python SDK).
- The August meetup builds as worked examples: the servo latch (aux pins moved from GPIO to PWM, 12 V regulated to 6 V payload side), the multispectral camera (clean power plus a native PWM trigger), the Starlink Mini (high voltage line through a regulator, unresolved link drop). Info notes and design files are T-11.
- Field lessons: the JMRRC dispenser's internal PCB corrupts PWM (bypass and wire direct), the dispenser browned out on the switched 12 V line and moved to HV.
- `task-grant-bounty/equipment/attachment/0002-*`: six attachment requirement documents (cargo, lidar, machine vision, camera, stabilized carrier, floodlight). Demand side context, list them as the attachments people want to build.
- `task-grant-bounty/pt3/electronics/0003-Attachment-Interface-PCB/`: the interface PCB history, design constraints, and the V1.4 BOM. Traceability anchor for every pinout claim.
- Interface conventions already written down elsewhere: relay semantics `Add HV`, `P1 Sig`, `P1 12V`, `12V Pay` (Pilot Handbook §2.8.5), the SSR power hierarchy (configuration guide §11), the payload IP range (configuration guide §0 network topology).

**What no document covers yet, and where each answer comes from**

| Gap | State today | Where the author gets it |
|---|---|---|
| Empty weight, battery weight, max payload mass | Documented nowhere. Issue #209 has asked since April | A weigh in at the next bench session, requested in this issue on day one |
| Pogo pad coordinates and a mechanical drawing | Only inside the V1.4 KiCad files | Vector extracted the coordinates for the #233 adapter board, ask for that extraction or re-extract from KiCad |
| Measured power limits | #234's numbers are traced from the schematic, PTC thermal derating unmeasured | One bench load test on the 12 V payload rail, requested in this issue on day one |
| Aux signal per port | The attach PCB silkscreen says `FMU_CH1` on every port. Netlist says bottom J31 = `FMU_CH1` (output 9), side 1 J29 = `FMU_CH7` (output 15), side 2 J30 = `FMU_CH8` (output 16) | Netlist, verified July 20, plus parameter readback (configuration guide §11.6) |
| Attachment CAN routing | #233 says CAN2 for all payloads. Netlist says J29 and J31 sit on CAN1, the flight critical bus at 1 Mbit, and only J30 is on CAN2 (RadarCAN, 500k, with the two NanoRadar sensors) | Netlist, verified July 20. Highest safety fact in the guide, a payload node on CAN1 shares the bus with the ESCs, the GNSS, and Remote ID |
| Ethernet reach, which ports carry it | Engineering Report reportedly inconsistent on C1/C2 versus C1/C2/C3 | Netlist plus the harness guide, continuity check at the bench |
| Hot swap rules | Nobody has written whether attachments may be connected or removed powered, or what the rails do across arm, disarm, and kill | Design intent from Erick, confirmed at the bench |
| Ethernet path from the pogo pins to the switch | Physical path lives only in harness guide fragments | Harness guide plus the Engineering Report network section |
| Side versus bottom port structural load limits | No ratings anywhere | CAD or FEA from Alperen, or a conservative documented limit marked as pending analysis |

About half of these close from existing files and people. The rest need one bench session and one weigh in, both of which can happen before the author has written a line.

**Chapters**

1. What a Quiver attachment is: the three ports, the hot swap concept, what exists today.
2. Mechanical interface: pogo geometry from V1.4, envelope, mass guidance, mounting, orientation.
3. Electrical contract: the pin table per port with real limits, the HV tap path, what trips and what browns out. Versioned to V1.4 as built, with a banner, so the coming interface redesign changes one chapter.
4. Power budgeting: three worked examples, a logic payload, a 25 W floodlight, the dispenser.
5. Control and data paths: PWM versus DroneCAN node versus Ethernet, when each is right, and the flight controller parameters each needs. The CAN1 warning lives here.
6. Flight controller integration: relay functions and labels, servo outputs, arming interactions, what the SSR hierarchy means for attachment power timing.
7. Software handoff: one page into the SDK guide, the template repository, and the Hub.
8. Validation: a bench checklist usable on its own (power draw, PWM verified on the pin, CAN enumeration, no rail sag), then the flight rules.
9. Lessons learned from the builds above.

**Milestones**

| | Deliverable | Amount |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | Chapters 1 to 3, every electrical claim traced to V1.4 KiCad, the netlist, or a cited issue | $250 |
| M2 | Chapters 4 to 9 complete, meetup builds written up as the examples, gap inputs incorporated with their source recorded | $350 |
| M3 | Review revisions merged, navigation entry, link checker and cspell green | $150 |

**Two inputs the team owes the author, not the other way round**

The weigh in (#209) and the 12 V rail load test from the gap table. The author asks for both in this issue on day one. If either is not delivered by M2, the guide publishes the schematic numbers with the gap marked open.

**Out of scope**

Resolving #234 (the power delivery redesign), building the #233 adapter board, the interface replacement decision, and the dispenser path decision. The guide documents today's interface and links the open threads.

**Acceptance criteria**

1. File at the target path, in the docs navigation beside the SDK guide (the two together are the Build on Quiver section), link checker and cspell green.
2. Every electrical claim traceable to V1.4 KiCad, the Main PCB sources, or a cited issue. No invented values.
3. Power limits match #234's traced numbers, or newer measurements with the measurement cited.
4. The bench validation checklist is usable on its own, without the rest of the guide.
5. Open engineering questions are marked open and never turned into requirements.
6. Every gap table input is sourced from the team or from a measurement, with the source recorded in the text.
7. Sign off from both reviewers in this issue.

**Claiming**

After the July bot claim wave on this line (an unsolicited 549 line guide arrived as a PR with payout first behavior and was not honored), claimants need an established Discord or forum presence before assignment. Say who you are and what you have read before you ask for M1.

**Acceptance and payment**
Each milestone is accepted by Thomas and Erick in this issue. Payouts batch monthly through the CSV airdrop flow. Board rules in `tasks.md`.

**What this report is**

The Quiver has three engineering reports (PT1, PT2, PT3) and a Dev Kit report, plus about thirty information notes under `task-grant-bounty/` across pt1, pt2, pt3, Dev-Kit, equipment, and general. Nobody can read that stack and come away knowing why the aircraft is the way it is. This report is the answer to that question: every design decision from the PT1 concept to the 2026 dev kit, what was chosen, what it replaced, why, and where the evidence is.

**What this report is not**

It is not a rewrite of the four reports. It is not an overview of the drone industry. It contains no sentence that cannot be traced to a file in this repository, a GitHub issue, a pull request, or a flight log. A paragraph that could appear in any UAV report is a paragraph that will be cut.

**The core artifact: the decision register**

A table, one row per design decision, in chronological order, with these columns:

| Column | What goes there |
|---|---|
| ID | D-001 upward |
| Phase | PT1, PT2, PT3, Dev Kit, or 2026 |
| Decision | One sentence. What was chosen. |
| Replaced | What it replaced, or "new" |
| Why | The reason in the words of the source, two sentences at most |
| Evidence | A link to the report section, information note, issue, PR, or log that records the decision |
| Status | Standing, superseded by D-xxx, or open |

Examples of rows that exist in the sources and that a reviewer will look for: the 25 kg MTOW and the propulsion selection (PT1 section 6), the move to DroneCAN ESCs and the Hobbywing X6 Plus G2, the Pixhawk 6C and the Arrow firmware build, the Main PCB and battery PCB split, the attachment interface and its V1.4 revision, the SSR and precharge power hierarchy, the two GNSS units and their roles, the native DroneCAN BMS on Bat2, the RPLidar S2 on SERIAL5, the two NanoRadar sensors on CAN2, the CubeNode ETH addressing, the Ethernet switches and the 2026 interference finding, the folding motor arms and the airframe modifications in the pt3 structural notes, the enclosure latch and sensor mounts, the transport case. Between sixty and one hundred rows is the expected size. Fewer than forty means the sources were not read.

**Milestone 0, the application, unpaid**

Post in this issue: the index of every source you found (reports, notes, issues) with one line each on what decisions it holds, and ten register rows in the format above chosen from at least three different phases. Reviewers check every citation. If a citation does not say what the row says, the sample fails and there is no assignment. If it passes, you are assigned and M1 opens. This gate exists because the reserved line has already drawn applications that read as generated text, and the register format is chosen so that generated text cannot pass it.

**Milestone 1, the register, $300**

The complete register merged as the first section of the report. Reviewers spot check at least twenty rows against their citations. One row that misstates its source sends the milestone back.

**Milestone 2, the narrative, $200**

One section per phase, two to four pages each, that reads the register as a story: what problem that phase was solving, which decisions it made, what it learned that the next phase used. Then the weight breakdown and the final build images still owed from the Dev Kit report (its Weight and Payload Summary is the starting point, the current airframe has to be weighed, issue #209). Then the open decisions at the end of 2026: the attachment interface replacement, the GPS interference mitigation, the dock. Review revisions merged, navigation entry, link checker and cspell green.

**Rules**

Every number has a source. Where two sources disagree, the row says so and cites both. Open questions stay open. No sentence about the future of aviation, the promise of open source, or what drones can do for humanity.

**The question**

Your full Quiver build has the same parts as the Houston unit: two GigaBlox switches beside the M9N, the CubeNode ETH, the Raspberry Pi. On the Houston unit, and on the West Texas unit, the M9N loses satellites with the switches installed and recovers when they are removed. Your build has never shown it, but nobody has checked whether your build was ever exercised the way the Houston unit is exercised in the field. This task settles that. The hypothesis is that the interference comes from Ethernet traffic, not from the switches merely being powered, so the test has to recreate the Houston operating setup, not just power the aircraft.

**Recreate the Houston setup, then read the GPS**

1. Switches installed and powered, CubeNode ETH up, Raspberry Pi up on the network, a laptop on the aircraft network. Mission Planner connected over TCP to the flight controller's Ethernet port (`192.168.144.51:5760`) with a live parameter session, so the Ethernet link is carrying traffic. Remote ID active on CAN (the db200 transmitting). `GPS2_TYPE 9` so the M9N is enabled.
2. Outdoors, open sky, aircraft on battery power, ten minute soak. Read and record for GPS 2: satellite count, HDOP, fix type, and `GPA.SAcc` from the log. Note the F9P (GPS 1) beside it as the control.
3. Same readings with the Mission Planner TCP session closed but the switches still powered. Then with both switches unplugged. Three rows, one change between each.
4. One flight in the first configuration (switches in, TCP session live, RID active), a few minutes of hover and gentle maneuvers. Paid from the campaign pool.
5. Parameter export on battery power after landing.

**Also record**

Where your two GigaBlox switches came from (official distributor or marketplace) and what the PHY chip on them reads, since sourcing is one of the open variables. How far the M9N sits from the nearest switch on your build, in millimeters. Any shielding, ferrites, or cable routing that differs from the Houston unit.

**Deliver**

A table of the three static rows plus the flight, the flight log uploaded to the flight tracking platform, the parameter export attached or committed under `docs/Operations/firmware/parameters/` with your unit's name, and the switch sourcing and distance notes. The answer to the title question, yes or no, with the numbers.

**Why it is worth two hours of your time**

Same parts, same layout, different builders, different outcomes. If your build is clean under the Houston operating setup, the fault is in build or configuration and the fix is cheap. If your build degrades once Ethernet traffic flows, the fault is in the design and the shielding work on the Houston unit is the right path. Either answer moves the devkit shipping blocker.

**Acceptance and payment**
Accepted by the Project Lead in this issue on the table, the log, and the export. The $150 pays through the monthly CSV airdrop. The flight is computed under the campaign mechanics. Board rules in `tasks.md`.

**What is being asked**

Define the V1 mechanics for paying people who fly. Until this exists the pool has sat untouched for five months while 23 validated flights were logged, and nobody who flew has been paid for flying. The September proposal committed to finalizing this in Phase 1 before any draw from the pool.

**What the page has to settle**

1. **What counts as a validated flight.** A log on the flight tracking platform, with the flight record fields filled, reviewed by someone other than the pilot. Say who that someone is by default.
2. **The rate.** A flat $ARROW amount per validated flight, with at most one multiplier for a flight that is part of a defined campaign (obstacle avoidance, endurance, an attachment test) versus a free flight. Keep the table to two rows.
3. **What is excluded.** Flights already paid under a bounty, flights that end in a failsafe or a crash, ferry hops, and flights by the retained lead that are inside the retainer's own operations (bench checks, hover checks after maintenance). Campaign flights by the lead with a defined deliverable are included, which is the T-03 case.
4. **The cap.** How much of the 10,000 one operator can draw in a phase, so the majority of the pool remains for future operators as the dev kit fleet grows, which is what the proposal promised the DAO.
5. **The clock.** Monthly, computed with the retro nominations, paid in the same airdrop batch.
6. **The first computation.** Apply it to the T-03 endurance flights as the worked example on the page.

**Why it is retainer work and not priced**

The lead retainer covers task board administration and treasury execution. This is both. Putting a price on it would be the retainer paying twice.

**Acceptance**
Accepted at the team call by adoption, recorded in the wiki notes for that call. No payment attached.

devGuideMd:
# Quiver SDK Developer Guide

**Version:** April 2026

---

## 1. System Overview

Quiver Hub is a cloud-hosted web application that provides real-time visualization, remote management, and data logging for UAV operations. The companion computer (Raspberry Pi) runs Python services that bridge the flight controller, payload devices, and Hub over HTTPS and WebSocket. Operators interact through the Hub web UI; the companion computer handles all local hardware communication and data forwarding autonomously.

The system supports five concurrent data pipelines: telemetry (MAVLink + UAVCAN), point cloud (LiDAR), camera (WebRTC via go2rtc), FC logs and OTA firmware, and custom payload apps. Each pipeline has a dedicated companion service, REST endpoint, and WebSocket broadcast channel.

---

## 2. Architecture

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        QUIVER HUB (Cloud)                       │
│  React UI · tRPC · REST API · Socket.IO · S3 · TiDB            │
└──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘
                           │ HTTPS / WSS (cellular or WiFi)
┌──────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┐
│              COMPANION COMPUTER  (Raspberry Pi)                  │
│  192.168.144.50                                                  │
│                                                                  │
│  Services:                                                       │
│    raspberry_pi_client.py   — Job polling & file delivery        │
│    telemetry_forwarder.py   — MAVLink + UAVCAN → Hub            │
│    logs_ota_service.py      — FC logs, OTA, diagnostics          │
│    camera_stream_service.py — go2rtc + Tailscale stream mgmt     │
│    siyi_camera_controller.py— Gimbal control (SIYI UDP SDK)      │
│                                                                  │
│  Connects to FC via Ethernet (MAVLink) and CAN bus (DroneCAN)    │
└──────────┬──────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
           │ Ethernet                     │ CAN bus
┌──────────┴──────────┐     ┌─────────────┴───────────────────────┐
│  FLIGHT CONTROLLER  │     │  PAYLOAD PORTS (C1 / C2 / C3)       │
│  192.168.144.51     │     │  Ethernet: 192.168.144.100–.199     │
│  ArduPilot + Lua    │     │  CAN: DroneCAN protocol             │
│  net_webserver.lua  │     │  Sensors, cameras, actuators        │
│  (port 8080)        │     └─────────────────────────────────────┘
└─────────────────────┘
```

---

## 3. Network Configuration

The Quiver network is flat — no DHCP runs on the Pi (Siyi firmware conflicts with DHCP servers). All IPs are static on the `192.168.144.0/24` subnet.

### Reserved Addresses (Do Not Use)

| IP | Device |
|---|---|
| 192.168.144.11 | Siyi air unit |
| 192.168.144.12 | Siyi ground unit |
| 192.168.144.20 | Android GCS (Siyi reserved) |
| 192.168.144.25 | Siyi A8 Mini camera |
| 192.168.144.60 | Siyi camera reserved |
| 192.168.144.50 | Raspberry Pi (companion computer) |
| 192.168.144.51 | Flight controller |

### Payload Port Assignments

Developer-assigned static range: `192.168.144.100` – `192.168.144.199`

| Port | Recommended IP |
|---|---|
| Bottom (J31) | 192.168.144.100 |
| Side 1 (J29) | 192.168.144.101 |
| Side 2 (J30) | 192.168.144.102 |

### Key Connections

| Path | Protocol | Details |
|---|---|---|
| Companion → Hub | HTTPS + WSS | REST API, Socket.IO (cellular/WiFi) |
| Companion → FC | Ethernet (MAVLink) | `192.168.144.51`, also CAN bus for DroneCAN |
| Companion → FC Web Server | HTTP | `http://192.168.144.51:8080` (net_webserver.lua, FC log access) |
| Companion → Payloads | Ethernet | `192.168.144.100–.199` via integrated switch |
| Companion → Siyi Camera | Ethernet | `192.168.144.25` (RTSP stream + UDP SDK) |
| Mission Planner → FC | RF telemetry | 915 MHz / 433 MHz radio (MAVLink) |

---

attachmentSpec.purpose:
This document defines the contract that Quiver payload attachments must implement to be compatible with `quiver.attachment` in the quiver-sdk.

There are two physical interfaces on every Quiver attachment port:
- **Ethernet** — high-bandwidth, for cameras, LiDAR, compute modules, custom sensors
- **CAN bus** — low-bandwidth, for actuators, simple sensors, battery monitors

Each has a different contract. CAN payloads use DroneCAN/UAVCAN (DSDL-typed messages — already standardized). Ethernet payloads need an explicit format contract, which this document defines.

A payload that implements this contract gets:
- Automatic typed discovery via `Attachment.scan()`
- Typed stream callbacks with schema-validated data
- Automatic QuiverHub App Builder integration (Hub knows which widget to render)
- mDNS-based name resolution (`sprayer.quiver.local`)
- Clean SDK API: `device.stream("scan")`, `device.command("start")`

A payload that does not implement this contract still works — but only as a raw byte pipe (`device.raw`).
